titleText.es: Quizás tampoco haya ternura en sus dedos, pero al menos ella da caña.
titleText.en: Maybe there's no tenderness in her fingertips either, but at least SHE puts out.
titleText.noteEn: This preserves the official English title text. The Spanish version uses dedos, literally “fingers,” and dar caña, a flexible colloquial expression for going hard or being intense, to carry the same sexually suggestive punchline.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Ya often means “already” or “now.” Before no, it instead marks a change from an earlier situation: ya no means “no longer” or “not anymore.”
Cierras comes from cerrar. In this present-time form, the stressed e in the middle changes to ie.

example.en: You close the door every night.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Beso can also be the noun “a kiss.” As a verb, beso is the present form used by a speaker to say “I kiss.”

example.es: Beso a mi pareja antes de salir.
example.en: I kiss my partner before leaving.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: your here; Spanish uses los before a body part whose owner is already clear
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish often uses el, la, los, or las before a body part when the context already makes its owner clear. The verb or another short word can identify the owner. Los is used before a masculine plural body-part word, as in los brazos, where English may naturally say “your arms.”
Había is the past form used to say that something existed or was present. In standard Spanish it stays singular even when the thing mentioned is plural.

example.es: Había tres sillas en la sala.
example.en: There were three chairs in the room.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Yema can mean an egg yolk, a plant bud, or the soft tip of a finger. The body-part meaning commonly appears in la yema del dedo or las yemas de los dedos.

example.es: Toca la pantalla con las yemas de los dedos.
example.en: Touch the screen with your fingertips.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word here; introduces the person, thing, or option tried after probar
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In probar con, con marks the chosen possibility that someone will try to see whether it works. English normally says “try” directly before that option, without a separate word for con.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that something used to be true or happen but does not anymore?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Put ya no before the verb to mean “no longer” or “not anymore.”
cardDefinitions.noteEn: No supplies the negative meaning, while ya shows that the situation has changed from before. The verb still changes normally for the person and time being discussed.

example.en: I no longer live in Madrid.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: Why does a verb such as cerrar change its middle e to ie in forms such as cierras?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: For certain verbs, change the stressed e in the verb's base to ie in most present-time forms.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The stressed e is the e in the syllable you naturally pronounce most strongly. The base is what remains after removing -ar, -er, or -ir. Cerrar has the base cerr-, which becomes cierr- in cierro, cierras, cierra, and cierran. The forms for nosotros and vosotros keep e: cerramos and cerráis. Only some e verbs follow this pattern, so learn the change with each verb.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: verbo + el/la/los/las + parte del cuerpo (dueño claro)
cardDefinitions.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes use the word for “the” before a body part where English uses “my,” “your,” or “their”?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: When the context already makes the owner clear, Spanish often uses el, la, los, or las before the body part instead of a possessive word such as mi or tu.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Choose el, la, los, or las to match the body part, not its owner: la mano is feminine singular, while los brazos is masculine plural. The verb or another short word in context can identify whose body part it is. If the owner would not otherwise be clear, Spanish can still use a possessive word.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say “there was” or “there were” in the past?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use había for both one thing and more than one thing.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: This use of haber says that something existed or was present; no person is doing an action. Standard Spanish keeps había singular: había una silla and había tres sillas. Do not change it to habían just because the following noun is plural.

example.es: Había mucha gente en el parque.
example.en: There were many people in the park.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: la yema del dedo / las yemas de los dedos
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you refer specifically to the soft tip or pad of a finger?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use la yema del dedo for one fingertip or las yemas de los dedos for more than one.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Yema has several meanings, including “egg yolk.” Adding del dedo or de los dedos selects the fingertip meaning. A word such as mis or tus can replace the article before dedos: las yemas de tus dedos means “your fingertips.”

example.es: Tengo frío en las yemas de los dedos.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: probar con + persona, cosa u opción
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that you will try a particular person, thing, or option to see whether it works?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of probar, then con, then the person, thing, or option being tried.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Probar by itself can mean to try, test, or taste. Con introduces the chosen possibility in this pattern. Only probar changes for the person and time; con stays unchanged.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: What song is the comic echoing before its punchline?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: The 1964 hit “You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin',” recorded by the Righteous Brothers.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The first two panels closely translate the song's opening romantic complaint. The last panel abruptly turns that sadness into a selfish, sexual suggestion.

regions.labelEs: YA NO CIERRAS LOS OJOS CUANDO BESO TUS LABIOS.

applications.explanationEn: Ya no marks a change from before, and cierras is the present verb describing what the listener no longer does.
Cerrar changes its stressed e to ie in the informal singular present form cierras.
Cierras already identifies the listener as the owner of the body part, so Spanish uses los before ojos; los matches the masculine plural word ojos.

regions.labelEs: Y LA TERNURA QUE HABÍA EN LAS YEMAS DE TUS DEDOS YA NO ESTÁ.

applications.explanationEn: Que links ternura to the added description, and había supplies the verb inside that description.
Había presents the tenderness as something that existed or was present in the past.
Las yemas names the soft tips, and de tus dedos identifies whose fingers they are part of.
Ya no marks a change from the earlier state, and está is the present verb describing what is no longer there.

regions.labelEs: QUIZÁS DEBERÍA PROBAR CON TU HERMANA.

applications.explanationEn: Debería keeps the full verb deber and adds the conditional ending -ía; with deber, that form makes the idea sound like a tentative “should.”
Debería carries the suggestion, while probar stays in its unchanged dictionary form as the proposed action.
Probar introduces trying an alternative, con marks the selected option, and tu hermana names that person.
